subject: biology
title: Reproduction
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Reproduction — AQA GCSE Biology (8461) specification, section 4.6.1.
meta_desc: GCSE Biology (AQA) practice covering Reproduction, specification section 4.6.1.
final_note: You worked through Reproduction — 50 specification statements.

concepts.def: The type of cell division that leads to non-identical cells being formed. It takes place in the reproductive organs to form gametes, and all the gametes produced are genetically different from each other.

The type of cell division that leads to identical cells being formed. It is the only division involved in asexual reproduction, and it is the division by which the new cell formed at fertilisation increases the number of cells.
Reproduction involving the joining (fusion) of male and female gametes. Because there is mixing of genetic information from two parents, it leads to variety in the offspring.

A sex cell that joins with another gamete at fertilisation. In animals the gametes are sperm and egg cells; in flowering plants they are pollen and egg cells. A gamete contains a single set of chromosomes.
Reproduction involving only one parent and no fusion of gametes. There is no mixing of genetic information, only mitosis is involved, and the offspring are genetically identical to the parent.
An offspring that is genetically identical to its parent. Clones are produced by asexual reproduction because only mitosis is involved and there is no mixing of genetic information.

Cells in the reproductive organs divide by meiosis to form gametes. Copies of the genetic information are made, then the cell divides twice to form four gametes, each with a single set of chromosomes and all genetically different from each other.
The joining of two gametes, which restores the normal number of chromosomes. Meiosis halves the chromosome number in the gametes, so fertilisation of two gametes brings the full number back.
After fertilisation the new cell divides by mitosis so the number of cells increases. As the embryo develops these cells differentiate, becoming specialised for different jobs.

Sexual reproduction produces variation in the offspring. If the environment changes, variation gives a survival advantage by natural selection. Natural selection can also be speeded up by humans in selective breeding to increase food production.

Asexual reproduction needs only one parent, so it is more time and energy efficient as there is no need to find a mate. It is faster than sexual reproduction and many identical offspring can be produced when conditions are favourable.

Some organisms reproduce by both methods depending on the circumstances. Malarial parasites reproduce asexually in the human host but sexually in the mosquito; many fungi reproduce asexually by spores but also sexually to give variation; many plants produce seeds sexually but also reproduce asexually by runners, such as strawberry plants, or bulb division, such as daffodils.
The chemical of which the genetic material in the nucleus of a cell is composed. DNA is a polymer made up of two strands forming a double helix, and it is contained in structures called chromosomes.
A structure in the nucleus that contains the DNA. Genes are carried as small sections of DNA along a chromosome.
A small section of DNA on a chromosome. Each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, to make a specific protein.
The entire genetic material of an organism. The whole human genome has now been studied and this will have great importance for medicine in the future.

concepts.term: Importance of understanding the human genome
concepts.def: Understanding the human genome matters for three reasons: the search for genes linked to different types of disease, the understanding and treatment of inherited disorders, and its use in tracing human migration patterns from the past.

The repeating unit from which the DNA polymer is made. Each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one of four different bases attached to the sugar, and DNA is made from four different nucleotides.
DNA contains four bases, A, C, G and T. One of these bases is attached to the sugar of each nucleotide, and the order of the bases carries the code.
A sequence of three bases is the code for a particular amino acid. The order of bases therefore controls the order in which amino acids are assembled to produce a particular protein.
The long strands of DNA consist of alternating sugar and phosphate sections. Attached to each sugar is one of the four bases.
In the complementary strands of the double helix a C is always linked to a G on the opposite strand, and a T to an A.
Proteins are synthesised on ribosomes, according to a template. Carrier molecules bring specific amino acids to add to the growing protein chain in the correct order.
When the protein chain is complete it folds up to form a unique shape. This unique shape enables proteins to do their job as enzymes, hormones or forming structures in the body such as collagen.
A change in DNA structure. Mutations occur continuously, and most do not alter the protein, or only alter it slightly so that its appearance or function is not changed.

concepts.term: Effect of a mutation on a protein
concepts.def: A few mutations code for an altered protein with a different shape. An enzyme may no longer fit the substrate binding site, or a structural protein may lose its strength.
Not all parts of DNA code for proteins. Non-coding parts of DNA can switch genes on and off, so variations in these areas of DNA may affect how genes are expressed.
One of the different forms a gene may have. Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene, such as fur colour in mice and red-green colour blindness in humans.
An allele that is always expressed, even if only one copy is present.
An allele that is only expressed if two copies are present, and therefore no dominant allele is present.
Describes an organism in which the two alleles present for a trait are the same.
Describes an organism in which the two alleles present for a trait are different.
The alleles present in an organism. The genotype operates at a molecular level to develop characteristics.
The characteristics that the genotype develops and that are expressed in the organism.
Most characteristics are a result of multiple genes interacting, rather than a single gene, so most phenotype features are not the result of single gene inheritance.

A diagram used to set out a genetic cross by combining the alleles carried by the gametes of each parent. The outcome can be expressed using direct proportion or simple ratios, and gives the probability of each genotype rather than a guaranteed result.

Disorders caused by the inheritance of certain alleles. Polydactyly, having extra fingers or toes, is caused by a dominant allele. Cystic fibrosis, a disorder of cell membranes, is caused by a recessive allele.

Screening embryos for the alleles that cause inherited disorders. It raises economic, social and ethical issues about which students should make informed judgements when given appropriate information.

Ordinary human body cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes. 22 pairs control characteristics only, but one of the pairs carries the genes that determine sex: in females the sex chromosomes are the same (XX) and in males they are different (XY).

mcqs.q: Which statement describes the cells formed by meiosis?
options: They are all genetically identical to each other.
They are all genetically different from each other.
There are two of them formed from the parent cell.
They each contain the full number of chromosomes.
mcqs.explain: Meiosis leads to non-identical cells being formed: all gametes are genetically different from each other.

mcqs.q: Which statement about sexual reproduction in a flowering plant is correct?
options: In plants, the gametes made by meiosis are all identical cells.
In plants, pollen and egg cells fuse, mixing genetic information.
In plants, one parent's gametes fuse without a second parent.
In plants, the gametes are made by mitosis in flower organs.
mcqs.explain: Sexual reproduction involves the joining (fusion) of male and female gametes, which in flowering plants are pollen and egg cells, and there is mixing of genetic information.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes asexual reproduction?
options: One parent is involved and meiosis forms identical cells.
One parent is involved and its gametes fuse together.
One parent is involved and the offspring show variation.
One parent is involved and only mitosis takes place.
mcqs.explain: Asexual reproduction involves only one parent, no fusion of gametes, and only mitosis, so the offspring are genetically identical clones.

mcqs.q: A cell in the reproductive organ of a mouse divides to form gametes. What is the result?
options: Two cells form by meiosis, both genetically different.
Four cells form by mitosis, all genetically identical.
Four cells form by meiosis, all genetically different.
Four cells form by meiosis, all genetically identical now.
mcqs.explain: Cells in reproductive organs divide by meiosis; the cell divides twice to form four gametes, all genetically different from each other.

mcqs.q: A body cell of a species contains 20 chromosomes. What happens to chromosome number during reproduction?
options: Meiosis gives gametes with 20; fertilisation reduces to 10.
Meiosis gives gametes with 10; fertilisation restores 20.
Meiosis gives two gametes with 10; fertilisation gives 20.
Meiosis gives gametes with 20; fertilisation restores 40.
mcqs.explain: Meiosis halves the number of chromosomes in gametes, so each gamete has a single set of 10, and fertilisation restores the full number of 20.

mcqs.q: What happens after two gametes join at fertilisation?
options: The new cell divides by meiosis, then cells differentiate.
The new cell divides by mitosis and then forms four gametes.
The new cell divides by mitosis and cells differentiate.
The new cell has half the chromosome number of gametes.
mcqs.explain: Gametes join at fertilisation to restore the normal number of chromosomes; the new cell divides by mitosis, the number of cells increases, and as the embryo develops cells differentiate.

mcqs.q: A grower has one healthy strawberry plant and wants many identical plants quickly. Why is reproduction by runners an advantage here?
options: Two parents share the work, so less time and energy are needed here.
One parent is needed and it is faster than sexual reproduction.
The offspring produced will show useful variation from the parent.
The plant can use only one method, so it cannot produce any seeds.
mcqs.explain: Advantages of asexual reproduction are that only one parent is needed, it is faster than sexual reproduction, and many identical offspring can be produced when conditions are favourable.

mcqs.q: Which statement about organisms that reproduce by both methods is correct?
options: Daffodils reproduce by bulb division, fusing gametes.
Malarial parasites reproduce only by one method, asexually.
Fungi reproduce asexually by spores to give variation.
Malarial parasites reproduce sexually in the mosquito.
mcqs.explain: Malarial parasites reproduce asexually in the human host, but sexually in the mosquito.

mcqs.q: A population of fungi lives in a habitat where conditions are beginning to change. Why may reproducing sexually be an advantage?
options: Asexual reproduction is what produces the variation needed in this habitat.
It is faster and uses less energy than reproducing asexually would be.
It produces variation, giving a survival advantage by natural selection.
Fungi can use only one method, so they have to reproduce sexually here.
mcqs.explain: Sexual reproduction produces variation in the offspring, and if the environment changes variation gives a survival advantage by natural selection.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes the structure of DNA?
options: A chemical stored loosely in the cell's cytoplasm
A polymer of four bases joined into two long strands
A polymer of amino acids joined in one long chain
A polymer of two strands forming a double helix
mcqs.explain: DNA is a polymer made up of two strands forming a double helix, contained in structures called chromosomes.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the genome of an organism?
options: The amino acids that make up an organism's DNA
The parts of the DNA that code for proteins
The genetic material found in the cytoplasm
The entire genetic material of an organism
mcqs.explain: The genome of an organism is the entire genetic material of that organism.

mcqs.q: A gene in a mouse is linked to brown fur. What does that gene code for?
options: The brown fur characteristic directly
A certain sequence of amino acids
One amino acid for each single base
An entire chromosome in the nucleus
mcqs.explain: Each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, to make a specific protein.

mcqs.q: Which of these is one of the uses of understanding the human genome?
options: Finding the gene that directly builds a feature
Removing non-coding DNA, which has no effect
Searching for genes linked to some diseases
Listing all genes that code for a protein
mcqs.explain: Understanding the human genome is important for the search for genes linked to different types of disease, the understanding and treatment of inherited disorders, and tracing human migration patterns from the past.

mcqs.q: DNA is a polymer. Which describes the repeating unit it is made from?
options: An amino acid joined to a sugar and phosphate group
A base joined directly on to the next base in the strand
Just one of the four different bases, A, C, G or T
A nucleotide of sugar, phosphate and one of four bases
mcqs.explain: DNA is a polymer made from four different nucleotides; each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one of four different bases attached to the sugar.

mcqs.q: A coding section of DNA contains 30 bases. How many amino acids does this code for?
options: 10, because three bases code for one amino acid
30, because one base codes for one amino acid
15, because each pair of bases codes for one acid
1, because the section codes for a characteristic
mcqs.explain: A sequence of three bases is the code for a particular amino acid, so 30 bases code for 10 amino acids.

mcqs.q: What forms the two long strands of a DNA molecule?
options: Nucleotides made only of the four bases
Alternating sugar and phosphate sections
Four bases joined end to end in order
Amino acids joined end to end in chains
mcqs.explain: The long strands of DNA consist of alternating sugar and phosphate sections, with one of the four bases attached to each sugar.

mcqs.q: In the complementary strands of DNA, how are the bases linked?
options: A is linked to C, while G is linked to T
Every base links to the next base along
Each base links to a matching identical base
C is linked to G, and T is linked to A
mcqs.explain: In the complementary strands a C is always linked to a G on the opposite strand and a T to an A.

mcqs.q: Where are proteins synthesised, and how do the amino acids reach the chain?
options: On ribosomes; carrier molecules bring the amino acids
On ribosomes; the DNA strand itself is the amino acids
In the cytoplasm's DNA; carrier molecules bring bases
In the nucleus; carrier molecules bring the amino acids
mcqs.explain: Proteins are synthesised on ribosomes, according to a template, and carrier molecules bring specific amino acids to add to the growing protein chain in the correct order.

mcqs.q: An enzyme is able to do its job because of which feature of the protein?
options: The characteristic that its gene codes for
The number of amino acids in its finished chain
The place in the nucleus where it was made
The unique shape it folds into at the end
mcqs.explain: When the protein chain is complete it folds up to form a unique shape, and this unique shape enables proteins to do their job as enzymes, hormones or structures such as collagen.

mcqs.q: Which statement about mutations is correct?
options: Each one alters the protein that is made.
Most do not alter the protein produced.
Only those in non-coding DNA have no effect.
Each one alters a characteristic directly.
mcqs.explain: Mutations occur continuously, and most do not alter the protein, or only alter it slightly so that its appearance or function is not changed.

mcqs.q: A mutation changes the shape of an enzyme. What is the likely effect?
options: The enzyme may no longer fit the substrate binding site.
Every other protein in the cell is altered in the same way.
There is no effect, because this DNA is non-coding DNA.
The enzyme still works, because only its length matters.
mcqs.explain: A few mutations code for an altered protein with a different shape: an enzyme may no longer fit the substrate binding site, or a structural protein may lose its strength.

mcqs.q: A genetic variant is found in a non-coding part of DNA. How may it influence the phenotype?
options: By altering how genes are switched on and off
It has no way of influencing the phenotype at all
By coding directly for a new characteristic
By altering the shape of every protein made
mcqs.explain: Non-coding parts of DNA can switch genes on and off, so variations in these areas of DNA may affect how genes are expressed.

mcqs.q: A mouse has two different alleles for fur colour. Which statement is correct?
options: It is homozygous, because two alleles are present here.
It is heterozygous, so the recessive allele is expressed.
It is heterozygous, so the dominant allele is shown.
It is heterozygous, so genotype equals phenotype.
mcqs.explain: If the alleles are different the organism is heterozygous, and a dominant allele is always expressed even if only one copy is present.

mcqs.q: A plant has the genotype Tt, where T is the dominant allele. What is its phenotype?
options: It shows T only if T is common in the population.
It shows the characteristic of the t allele only.
Its phenotype is written as the full genotype Tt.
It shows the characteristic of the T allele.
mcqs.explain: A dominant allele is always expressed, even if only one copy is present, so the alleles present develop the characteristic coded by T.

mcqs.q: Two heterozygous mice (Bb) are crossed, where B is dominant. Which ratio of phenotypes does a Punnett square predict?
options: 3 with the dominant characteristic to 1 without
1 with the dominant characteristic to 3 without
4 with the dominant characteristic to 0 without
2 with the dominant characteristic and 2 without
mcqs.explain: The Punnett square gives BB, Bb, Bb and bb. The dominant allele is expressed in the first three, so the predicted ratio is 3 to 1.

mcqs.q: In a family tree, two parents who do not have cystic fibrosis have a child who does. What does this show?
options: The allele causing the disorder is dominant.
The parents' genotype matches their phenotype.
Each parent carries one recessive allele.
Only one parent carries the recessive allele.
mcqs.explain: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele, which is only expressed if two copies are present, so each unaffected parent must carry one copy to pass on.

mcqs.q: A student uses a single gene cross to predict a person's height. Why is this prediction unreliable?
options: Every characteristic is controlled by one single gene here.
Most characteristics result from multiple genes interacting.
A gene codes directly for the characteristic, not protein.
A single cross gives exact numbers of offspring produced.
mcqs.explain: Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene, but most characteristics are a result of multiple genes interacting rather than a single gene.

mcqs.q: In mice, black fur (B) is dominant to brown (b). A black mouse is crossed with a brown mouse and some brown offspring are produced. What was the black parent's genotype?
options: BB, since its two alleles are the same
bb, since a b allele was expressed here
Bb, since it passed on a b allele
BB, since B is the more common allele
mcqs.explain: A brown offspring must be bb, so it received a b allele from each parent. The black parent expressed B but also carried b, so its genotype was Bb.

mcqs.q: Which alleles cause polydactyly and cystic fibrosis?
options: Polydactyly dominant; cystic fibrosis recessive
Both are dominant, as the disorders are common
Both are recessive, as one copy is enough here
Polydactyly recessive; cystic fibrosis is dominant
mcqs.explain: Polydactyly (having extra fingers or toes) is caused by a dominant allele, and cystic fibrosis (a disorder of cell membranes) is caused by a recessive allele.

mcqs.q: A couple are offered embryo screening. Which of these is an ethical issue they might consider?
options: Whether one gene controls all the embryo's traits
Whether the screening test is medically accurate
Whether rejecting an embryo with an allele is right
Whether a gene codes for a trait or for a protein
mcqs.explain: Embryo screening raises economic, social and ethical issues, and whether it is right to reject an embryo because of the alleles it carries is an ethical judgement.

mcqs.q: What do ordinary human body cells contain?
options: 23 pairs of chromosomes, one pair determining sex
23 chromosomes in total, one of them determining sex
23 pairs of chromosomes, with XY in every female
23 pairs of chromosomes, all from the mother's egg
mcqs.explain: Ordinary human body cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs control characteristics only, but one of the pairs carries the genes that determine sex.

mcqs.q: A genetic cross is carried out between XX and XY parents. What does it predict about the offspring?
options: 1 female to 1 male, so a 50% chance of each
Exactly 2 girls and 2 boys in four babies
All female, as the egg cell decides sex
3 females to 1 male, as X is dominant here
mcqs.explain: The cross gives XX, XX, XY and XY, a simple ratio of 1 female to 1 male, so there is a 50% probability of each sex.
